claims.statement: `cqg parse <raw_dir> --out <parsed_dir>` writes exactly two files per document: `<doc_id>.md`, the markdown as it will be ingested into RAG and editable by hand, and `<doc_id>.parse.json`, the sidecar carrying blocks, images, parse_confidence, markdown_hash, schema_version and provenance.

`parse` refuses an input folder that is already a parsed_input/ with the message "<dir> est deja un parsed_input/ : rien a parser.", and refuses an output folder identical to the source folder, because writing parsed markdown beside its own sources would make the folder ambiguous for every later command.

Because doc_id is the file stem, two sources sharing a stem — a .docx next to its PDF export — would both claim the same parsed markdown; `_refuse_colliding_doc_ids` raises before anything is written, naming both paths, since one would otherwise be skipped as already parsed and --force would overwrite rather than recover it.

The sidecar is not optional because the deterministic inventory counts blocks to decide which criteria are `na`: a markdown read without its sidecar would show zero tables and zero images, flip the structure criteria to `na`, and move the document's score for a reason foreign to the quality of the document.

The parsed markdown is written with write_bytes on a UTF-8 encoding and read back with read_bytes().decode("utf-8"), never through universal-newline decoding, and no trailing newline is appended — because that exact string is what non_alpha_fraction, token_count and duplicate_line_fraction are computed on, and a CR rewritten as LF would shift all three.

A folder is detected as a parsed_input/ solely by the presence of at least one `*.parse.json`; a `.md` file never decides the mode, because .md is both a supported source format and the output of parsing, so a folder of hand-written notes stays a legitimate raw corpus.

A folder holding both sidecars and raw sources raises "Dossier ambigu: ... contient a la fois des documents parses ... et des sources brutes ... Separez raw_input/ et parsed_input/." rather than being guessed at, because scoring it as raw would re-parse the markdown exports and ignore the sidecars while scoring it as parsed would drop the sources.

Parsed entries are listed sorted on the file name rather than the stem, to match the order triage_corpus gives raw sources, because that ordering drives the row order of corpus_report.xlsx and the grouping of corpus_redundancy.json and neither should depend on which path the corpus took; orphan sidecars are included in the listing so a document whose markdown was deleted is still reported.

Reading a parsed entry is total — every folder state yields a document and a list of flags rather than an exception: `manually_edited` on a markdown_hash mismatch, `missing_sidecar` for a markdown alone, `missing_markdown` for an orphan sidecar, `invalid_sidecar` for a sidecar that is not valid JSON, `sidecar_schema_unsupported:<n>` for a schema_version newer than this cqg understands, and `renamed:<original_doc_id>` when the sidecar's doc_id disagrees with the file name.

A parsed markdown re-saved in another encoding is decoded with errors="replace", so the damage becomes U+FFFD — which cid_failure_fraction already counts, penalising parse_confidence and flagging the document — the same precedent _plain_text_extraction set for .txt/.md sources, and it arrives flagged manually_edited as well since the file genuinely changed.

When the sidecar's recorded doc_id disagrees with the file name, the file name wins and the original is reported as `renamed:<original_doc_id>`, because the file name is what indexes the folder and names the score file — a duplicated pair edited into a variant would otherwise write the same score file twice and one copy would silently overwrite the other.
Document identifiers containing spaces, accents and parentheses round-trip through the parsed_input/ layout unchanged, sidecar file name included.

`parse` skips a document already present in the output folder rather than overwriting it, because the markdown may have been corrected by hand and a silent re-parse would discard that work; --force is the explicit way to ask for the overwrite, and passing --force to `run` or `golden` prints that it is without object and is ignored.

On a skipped document `parse` compares the source's current sha256 with the one recorded in provenance and collects a mismatch into `source_changed`, which the CLI prints as "Source modifiee depuis le parsing (relancer avec --force pour reparser)" — reported and never acted on, because choosing between the human's edit and the new source version is the human's call.

On a hand-edited markdown the text blocks are recomputed from what the human wrote while every non-text block and the image geometry are kept from the sidecar; paragraphs are split on blank lines with CRLF accepted, because a hand-edited markdown is the one likely to come back from a Windows editor, and each recomputed block is given page=0, the sentinel the docling and docx extractions already use, because after an edit the page a paragraph came from is unknown and claiming page 1 would invent a location.

A regression test asserts the consequence directly: editing the prose of a parsed .docx that carries a real table raises manually_edited while leaving the set of `na` criteria and the global score identical, with a further assertion that the table criteria were live in the first place so the equality cannot hold trivially.

An unsupported_format document crosses the boundary as an entry with an empty markdown whose category is preserved in provenance, and an unreadable document crosses the same way, so `run` raises the same `unsupported_format:<type>` or `unreadable` flag it would have raised on the raw folder.
On a parsed_input/ the scoring path opens no source file at all: the markdown and its sidecar are the whole input.

`parse` prints every error it collected and exits with code 1, and a folder it refuses outright — ambiguous, self-overwriting or with colliding document names — prints an explanatory operator message and exits with code 2, because parsed_input/ feeds the scoring step and a partial output that looks like a success is how a document silently disappears from a report.

A non-regression test pins the whole split: over a corpus of four documents — a text PDF, an illustrated PDF, a Markdown note and a deliberately corrupt PDF — `parse` followed by `run <parsed_input>` produces *.score.json files strictly identical to a direct `run <raw>`, parameterised over the enriched and non-enriched cases, with the enriched split run deliberately scoring with enrichment off so the equality is carried by the markdown `parse` wrote.
